docs.text: Driver DYNAMIXEL Driver ¶ A C++20 bus-master driver for ROBOTIS DYNAMIXEL servos. It speaks protocol 1.0 and 2.0 over a half-duplex UART, finds the servos, reads and writes their control tables by name, and runs Sync, Bulk and Fast reads, on any MCU. Quickstart API guide Source on GitHub The driver has no platform code. You give it a small class that moves bytes on your UART; it does the rest: packet framing and byte stuffing, CRC-16 and checksums, finding the reply in the received bytes, retries, the per-register decoding of 9 families of servos and the per-servo outcome of a Sync or Fast read. Smart servo DYNAMIXEL ROBOTIS Function Servo with a control table of registers; position, velocity, current and PWM control Interface Half-duplex TTL or RS-485 UART, 8N1, 9 600 to 4.5 Mbit/s; one line shared by every servo Protocols 2.0 (CRC-16, byte stuffing) and 1.0 (checksum); one per bus Instructions Ping, Read, Write, Reg Write, Action, Reboot, Factory Reset, Clear, Backup, Sync, Bulk and the Fast reads Catalogue 47 model numbers in 9 control-table families: AX, RX, DX, MX (1.0 and 2.0), XL-320, XL330, XL430, XM, XH, XD, XW What you get ¶ One object per bus. DYNAMIXEL<YourPort> takes a reference to your port and does no I/O until EnsureInitialized() . See API guide . Errors you can act on. Every call returns Result<T> with an Error such as Timeout , LineFault , EchoMismatch or DeviceError , and the raw reply is kept for inspection. See API guide . Typed registers. ReadRegister() , WriteRegister() and ReadFeedback() use one name per register for every family, with decoding, range checks and units. See Control tables . One outcome per servo. A Sync, Bulk or Fast read fills a DeviceReply per ID: a truncated or corrupted packet still delivers the servos whose part arrived whole. A safe stop. DisableTorque() is never refused: not before the bus is initialised, not when the input flush fails. Zero-overhead portability. The port is a CRTP class checked by a concept: five hooks, plus optional baud and logging hooks found at compile time. See Porting . No heap, no exceptions, no RTTI. The host tests build with -fno-exceptions -fno-rtti . See Contract . Where to start ¶ You want to Read Move a servo from your PC or MCU in a few minutes Quickstart Wire the bus and set the direction control Hardware Write the UART port for your platform Porting Know the packets and the reply search Protocol Know the registers of your servo Control tables Read, write and read many servos at once API guide Find out why nothing answers Troubleshooting See what is tested, fuzzed and mutated Testing and CI Status ¶ Version 0.1.0. The behaviour is checked against a model of the bus that is written separately from the driver, by unit tests, fuzzing and mutation testing ( Testing and CI ). It has not been run against a servo yet. Four points the e-Manual does not specify are listed in the Contract . The shape of the API ¶ Group Calls Lifecycle EnsureInitialized() , IsInitialized() , Deinitialize() , Resync() , ApplyConfig() , GetConfig() Discovery Ping() , Identify() , BroadcastPing() , ScanIds() Raw registers Read() , Write() , RegWrite() , Action() Typed registers ReadRegister() , WriteRegister() , ReadFeedback() , SetTorque() , SetGoalPosition() Many servos SyncRead() , FastSyncRead() , BulkRead() , FastBulkRead() , SyncWrite() , BulkWrite() The safe stop DisableTorque() , DisableTorqueAll() , DisableTorqueEach() , DisableTorqueAt() Setup of a servo SetId() , SetServoBaudRate() , ChangeBusBaud() , SetStatusReturnLevel() Destructive FactoryReset() , Reboot() , Clear() , Backup() Diagnostics GetLastReply() , GetLatchedAlert() , ClearLatchedAlert() , GetStats() , ResetStats() , GetLastRequest() Tables Info() , FindModel() , FamilyOf() , Indirect() , BaudValueFor() (free functions) Every call that uses the bus returns Result<T> : check ok() (or the bool conversion) and read value , or read error . Result is [[nodiscard]] , so an unchecked call is a compiler warning. Every call blocks until its reply is complete or its deadlines have passed ( why ). Initialise ¶ dynamixel :: Error BringUp ( Servos & servos ) { // The one entry point: starts the UART on the first call, then returns Ok with no I/O. After a // failure the next call starts again from the beginning. const auto r = servos . EnsureInitialized (); if ( ! r ) { std :: printf ( "DYNAMIXEL init: %s \n " , dynamixel :: ToString ( r . error )); } return r . error ; } The constructor stores the port and the configuration ( Config{} unless you pass one) and does no I/O. EnsureInitialized() is the one way to start the driver: it checks the configuration, brings the UART up through your port and applies Config::baud . It sends nothing on the bus, so it succeeds with no servo connected. Once it has succeeded, EnsureInitialized() returns Ok at once with no I/O, so a caller can call it before every use. After a failure the driver stays uninitialised and the next call starts again from the beginning. Before it succeeds every call that uses the bus returns NotInitialized and sends nothing; argument and permission errors ( InvalidArgument , Unsupported , NotPermitted ) come first, and the torque-off calls are never refused ( Contract ). Find the servos ¶ dynamixel :: Result < uint32_t > FindServos ( Servos & servos , std :: span < dynamixel :: PingInfo > found ) { // Protocol 2.0: one broadcast ping, every servo answers in ID order. const auto all = servos . BroadcastPing ( found ); if ( all . ok () && ( all . value > 0U )) { return all ; } // Protocol 1.0 has no broadcast answers: ping the IDs one by one. return servos . ScanIds ( 1 , 20 , found ); } Ping(id) answers with the model number and firmware; PingInfo::family is the control table that model uses ( Family::Generic for a model the catalogue does not list). BroadcastPing() asks every servo at once in protocol 2.0; the servos answer in ID order, each within Config::broadcast_timeout_us . Protocol 1.0 has no broadcast answers: ScanIds(first, last, found) pings each ID in turn and takes a missing one as absent. A protocol 1.0 ping does not return the model; Identify(id) pings and then reads the model number and firmware. Move and read by register name ¶ dynamixel :: Error GoTo ( Servos & servos , dynamixel :: ServoRef servo , int32_t counts ) { if ( auto r = servos . SetTorque ( servo , true ); ! r ) { return r . error ; } if ( auto r = servos . SetGoalPosition ( servo , counts ); ! r ) { return r . error ; } const auto feedback = servos . ReadFeedback ( servo ); // position, velocity, load, voltage, temperature return feedback . error ; } A ServoRef is an ID and a Family . The typed calls look up the register in the family's table, check that the value fits and that the register is writable, encode it (little-endian, two's complement or sign-magnitude as the family does) and send it; reads decode the same way. ReadFeedback() returns position, velocity, load or current, voltage and temperature in one transfer. A family without the register returns Unsupported ; a value that does not fit returns InvalidArgument . Nothing is sent in either case. For a register the table does not name, use the raw Read() and Write() with an address and bytes, on any family including Generic . RegWrite() stores the write in the servo and Action() executes the stored writes of every servo together, so a group of servos starts moving on the same packet. Read many servos at once ¶ dynamixel :: Error ReadAllPositions ( Servos & servos , std :: span < int32_t > positions ) { const std :: array < uint8_t , 3 > ids { 1 , 2 , 3 }; std :: array < uint8_t , 12 > raw {}; std :: array < dynamixel :: DeviceReply , 3 > replies {}; // Present Position of the X430 family: address 132, four bytes. Fast Sync Read answers in one // packet. const auto r = servos . FastSyncRead ( 132 , 4 , ids , raw , replies ); for ( std :: size_t i = 0 ; ( i < replies . size ()) && ( i < positions . size ()); ++ i ) { if ( replies [ i ]. result == dynamixel :: Error :: Ok ) { // each servo has its own outcome positions [ i ] = static_cast < int32_t > ( static_cast < uint32_t > ( raw [ 4U * i ]) | ( static_cast < uint32_t > ( raw [( 4U * i ) + 1U ]) << 8U ) | ( static_cast < uint32_t > ( raw [( 4U * i ) + 2U ]) << 16U ) | ( static_cast < uint32_t > ( raw [( 4U * i ) + 3U ]) << 24U )); } } return r . error ; } SyncRead() asks a list of servos for the same registers; they answer one after another. FastSyncRead() (protocol 2.0, firmware that lists it: SupportsFastRead() ) has them answer inside one packet. BulkRead() and FastBulkRead() take a different address and length per servo. All four fill the caller's buffer, one slice per servo in request order, and one DeviceReply per servo: DeviceReply Meaning result Ok , or why this servo's data is not valid: Timeout (silent, or its part did not arrive), Crc , DeviceIdMismatch , DeviceError , DeviceFault error_byte The raw error byte, when a packet arrived alert The hardware alert flag of that servo The call's own Result says whether the exchange worked; it can be Ok while a servo is Timeout , and a damaged packet still delivers the servos whose part was whole. Read the data only of the servos that are Ok . SyncWrite() and BulkWrite() send one packet to many servos and get no answer; Ok means sent. Stop safely ¶ void EmergencyStop ( Servos & servos ) { // Never refused: no initialisation needed, no consent flag, three attempts per servo. // One broadcast packet; the servos do not answer a broadcast, so confirm with a read afterwards. static_cast < void > ( servos . DisableTorqueAll ( dynamixel :: Family :: X430 )); } DisableTorque(servo) , DisableTorqueAll(family) , DisableTorqueEach(servos) and DisableTorqueAt(id, address) write Torque Enable to 0. They are never refused for the driver's state: no initialisation is needed (they start the port themselves and set the bus baud rate), no consent flag is checked, and a failing input flush does not stop the write (the call then reports Bus after sending). Each servo gets up to three attempts: one is enough when a trusted answer confirms it; when no answer can (status return level below 2, or the broadcast form, which no servo answers) all three are sent, because one lost packet would leave the torque on, and Ok then means "sent", so confirm with a read if the stop matters. The only refusals, which send nothing, are an argument the bus protocol does not have (an ID out of range, an address above 255 in protocol 1.0, a family that does not speak the bus protocol) and a port that cannot start. DisableTorqueEach() tries every servo and returns only the first error; call DisableTorque() for each servo when you need to know which one failed. A family with no torque register ( Generic , a model the catalogue does not list) is refused by DisableTorque() and DisableTorqueAll() , because the driver cannot know the address: use DisableTorqueAt(id, address) with the Torque Enable address from that servo's own control table (64 on the X series, 24 on AX/RX/DX); it is the same stop path, so a Generic servo has the same safety stop. Take the address from the e-Manual's control table for the exact model and firmware. The call writes one byte, 0, at whatever address you give, and with ID 254 it does so to every servo on the bus: a wrong address can set every ID to 0, change the baud rate or silence the servos (on an X-series servo, address 7 is the ID, 8 the baud rate and 68 the status return level), and 24 is a different register on protocol 2.0 X-series servos than on AX/RX/DX. Safe uses are a torque address read from the table of the servo in hand, one servo ID at a time, tested once on the bench. Reboot() is sent the same way. The time a stop can take is bounded, not short: in each attempt the first read waits the reply timeout and every later read the gap timeout, for at most 4 * FrameBytes + 16 reads, and there are three attempts. A line that gives one byte per read can therefore hold a stop for up to 3 * (Config::reply_timeout_us + (4 * FrameBytes + 15) * Config::gap_timeout_us) (the timeouts are held inside 100 microseconds to 1 second on this path). A test pins this formula. Use short timeouts when the stop must return quickly. Alerts ¶ void CheckAlerts ( Servos & servos ) { const auto temperature = servos . ReadRegister ({ 1 , dynamixel :: Family :: X430 }, dynamixel :: Reg :: PresentTemperature ); if ( temperature . ok () && servos . GetLastReply (). alert ) { // Bit 7 of the error byte: the servo reports a hardware error. The data is valid. std :: printf ( "servo 1 alert, error byte 0x%02X \n " , static_cast < unsigned > ( servos . GetLatchedAlert (). error_byte )); servos . ClearLatchedAlert (); } } A servo with a hardware error pending sets the alert flag in its reply (bit 7 of the error byte in protocol 2.0; the voltage, temperature and overload flags in protocol 1.0). With AlertPolicy::Report (the default) the call succeeds with valid data and the alert is latched until ClearLatchedAlert() ; with AlertPolicy::Fail the call returns DeviceFault and no data. Read Reg::HardwareErrorStatus for the cause. Handle errors ¶ const char * Describe ( dynamixel :: Error e ) { switch ( e ) { case dynamixel :: Error :: Timeout : return "no answer: ID, baud rate, protocol or wiring" ; case dynamixel :: Error :: LineFault : return "the line is stuck or floating: check power and the direction control" ; case dynamixel :: Error :: EchoMismatch : return "the echo differs: another talker on the bus, or the loopback setting is wrong" ; case dynamixel :: Error :: DeviceError : return "the servo refused the instruction: see GetLastReply().error_byte" ; case dynamixel :: Error :: NotPermitted : return "destructive instruction: set Config::allow_destructive on purpose" ; default : return dynamixel :: ToString ( e ); } } Signal Meaning What to do Error::Timeout No complete reply The servo's power, ID, rate, protocol, the direction control; raise reply_timeout_us Error::LineFault The line is stuck or floating Power, ground, the half-duplex stage; then Resync() Error::EchoMismatch The echo differs from the request Another talker, or Config::echo is wrong Error::Crc , InvalidReply A damaged or malformed reply The rate, the ground, the cable; Resync() Error::DeviceError The servo refused the instruction GetLastReply().error_byte ; often an EEPROM write with the torque on Error::DeviceFault A hardware alert with AlertPolicy::Fail Reg::HardwareErrorStatus Error::NotPermitted A destructive call without consent Config::allow_destructive , on purpose Error::Bus Your port reported a failure The port and the UART Every value, with the calls that return it, is on the Contract page, and Troubleshooting goes through each. dynamixel::ToString() names an error for a log. Reset a servo ¶ dynamixel :: Error ResetToFactory ( MyPort & port , dynamixel :: Config config ) { config . allow_destructive = true ; // the one switch that unlocks reset, restore and broadcast ID writes static Servos servos ( port , config ); return servos . FactoryReset ( 1 , dynamixel :: ResetOption :: KeepIdAndBaud ). error ; } Factory Reset, Control Table Restore ( Backup() with BackupOption::Restore ), Clear() and an ID write to every servo ( SetId() with the broadcast ID) change or erase what a servo keeps, so they return NotPermitted unless Config::allow_destructive is set. A reset can change the ID and baud rate: ResetOption::KeepIdAndBaud keeps them. After a reset or a reboot the driver waits Config::reboot_wait_us before the next call. Backup() with BackupOption::Store is not behind that flag: it overwrites the servo's backup area but nothing the servo runs on. SetStatusReturnLevel() adopts a lower level when the answer to its write is silent, because the servo stops answering at the new level. A lost write looks the same, so the driver logs a warning in that case: read the register back to verify. Diagnostics ¶ For bring-up and fault finding the driver keeps what it saw (handbook KB-CPP-119, KB-CPP-129), with no I/O: Call What it gives GetLastRequest() The bytes of the last instruction packet, as put on the line GetLastReply() The decoded error byte of the last status packet GetLatchedAlert() , ClearLatchedAlert() The first alert since the last clear GetStats() , ResetStats() Transactions, retries, timeouts, CRC errors, garbage bytes, line faults Shut down ¶ void PowerDown ( Servos & servos ) { // No bus traffic: the servos keep their state. Stop them first when they must not move. static_cast < void > ( servos . DisableTorqueAll ( dynamixel :: Family :: X430 )); static_cast < void > ( servos . Deinitialize ()); } After Deinitialize() every call that uses the bus returns NotInitialized until the next EnsureInitialized() . Deinitialize() sends nothing: the servos keep their state, so stop them first when they must not move. Next: Configuration .

docs.text: void EmergencyStop ( Servos & servos ) { // Never refused: no initialisation needed, no consent flag, three attempts per servo. // One broadcast packet; the servos do not answer a broadcast, so confirm with a read afterwards. static_cast < void > ( servos . DisableTorqueAll ( dynamixel :: Family :: X430 )); } DisableTorque(servo) , DisableTorqueAll(family) , DisableTorqueEach(servos) and DisableTorqueAt(id, address) write Torque Enable to 0. They are never refused for the driver's state: no initialisation is needed (they start the port themselves and set the bus baud rate), no consent flag is checked, and a failing input flush does not stop the write (the call then reports Bus after sending). Each servo gets up to three attempts: one is enough when a trusted answer confirms it; when no answer can (status return level below 2, or the broadcast form, which no servo answers) all three are sent, because one lost packet would leave the torque on, and Ok then means "sent", so confirm with a read if the stop matters. The only refusals, which send nothing, are an argument the bus protocol does not have (an ID out of range, an address above 255 in protocol 1.0, a family that does not speak the bus protocol) and a port that cannot start. DisableTorqueEach() tries every servo and returns only the first error; call DisableTorque() for each servo when you need to know which one failed. A family with no torque register ( Generic , a model the catalogue does not list) is refused by DisableTorque() and DisableTorqueAll() , because the driver cannot know the address: use DisableTorqueAt(id, address) with the Torque Enable address from that servo's own control table (64 on the X series, 24 on AX/RX/DX); it is the same stop path, so a Generic servo has the same safety stop. Take the address from the e-Manual's control table for the exact model and firmware. The call writes one byte, 0, at whatever address you give, and with ID 254 it does so to every servo on the bus: a wrong address can set every ID to 0, change the baud rate or silence the servos (on an X-series servo, address 7 is the ID, 8 the baud rate and 68 the status return level), and 24 is a different register on protocol 2.0 X-series servos than on AX/RX/DX. Safe uses are a torque address read from the table of the servo in hand, one servo ID at a time, tested once on the bench. Reboot() is sent the same way. The time a stop can take is bounded, not short: in each attempt the first read waits the reply timeout and every later read the gap timeout, for at most 4 * FrameBytes + 16 reads, and there are three attempts. A line that gives one byte per read can therefore hold a stop for up to 3 * (Config::reply_timeout_us + (4 * FrameBytes + 15) * Config::gap_timeout_us) (the timeouts are held inside 100 microseconds to 1 second on this path). A test pins this formula. Use short timeouts when the stop must return quickly.

The layers, one of them yours Figure description and sources Top to bottom, each arrow is a call. Your application calls one object, whose public calls are listed from the umbrella header in inc/. The core turns each call into register reads and writes and hands them to the port contract (the CRTP base in inc/*_interface.hpp), which forwards them, at compile time, to the hooks of the port class you write; your port moves the bytes on the bus. The notes on the right say which layers stay the same on every MCU and which one you write. A library without a port contract has only the first two layers. Layers ¶ Layer Files Owns Core inc/dynamixel.hpp , src/dynamixel.ipp Lifecycle, transactions, retries, Sync, Bulk and Fast reads, typed registers, the safe stop Protocol inc/dynamixel_protocol.hpp Packet builder ( FrameWriter ), byte stuffing, CRC-16, checksum, the reply search ( Scan ), the Fast packet parts Control tables inc/dynamixel_tables.hpp The register table of each family, the 47 model numbers, units, the baud schemes, indirect addresses Types inc/dynamixel_types.hpp Error , Result<T> , Config and its presets, Feedback , DeviceReply , Stats , Validate() Port contract inc/dynamixel_uart_interface.hpp The CRTP base, the UartPort concept, the bus requirements Platform port Your class The UART bring-up, byte transfers, the half-duplex direction, delays, optionally the baud rate and logging Kconfig layer inc/dynamixel_kconfig.hpp Optional: a Config from ESP-IDF menuconfig The protocol and table layers are pure functions of bytes and constants: they have no port and are tested alone. One call through the layers ¶ sequenceDiagram participant App as Your code participant Core as DYNAMIXEL<Port> participant Port as Your port App->>Core: ReadRegister({1, X430}, PresentPosition) Note over Core: table lookup: address 132, 4 bytes Core->>Port: Write(instruction packet) Port-->>Core: true (last stop bit sent) Core->>Port: Read(buffer, max, reply_timeout_us) Port-->>Core: n bytes Note over Core: Scan: header, length, instruction, CRC-16 Note over Core: error byte, ID, parameter count Core-->>App: Result<int32_t>{2048, Ok} A transaction is one Write() of the whole packet, then one or more Read() calls until a complete, valid status packet is in the buffer or a deadline passes. A ping or a read that fails for a bad or missing reply is repeated up to Config::retries times; a write is never repeated, because a write whose reply was lost may have been carried out ( Protocol ). Design choices ¶ CRTP, not virtual functions. The port is a template parameter constrained by the UartPort concept, so every call is resolved at compile time and a missing hook is a compile error that names it. Optional hooks by requires . SetBaudRate and Log are detected with C++20 requires in one place, and their exact signature is checked: a hook that is declared wrongly does not compile. A missing SetBaudRate() leaves the port's own rate and makes ChangeBusBaud() return Unsupported ; a missing Log() logs nothing. No I/O in the constructor. Construction cannot fail, so the driver can be a static or a member of a handler. One error type. Result<T> carries a value and an Error ; nothing throws and nothing returns a bare bool . On failure the value is T{} . Fixed buffers. The driver owns one transmit and one receive buffer of FrameBytes bytes (512 by default, 64 to 4096) and a 64-byte scratch buffer; a transfer that does not fit returns InvalidArgument before anything is sent. Nothing allocates. One outcome per servo. A multi-servo read does not collapse to one error: each DeviceReply carries the servo's own result, error byte and alert flag, and the call's Result says only whether the exchange as a whole worked. Independent test model. The host tests talk to a model of the bus written separately from the driver, so a misreading of the e-Manual in the driver is not copied into the test ( Testing and CI ). Why there is no non-blocking API ¶ Every call blocks until its reply is complete or its deadlines have passed. The driver has no Start and Poll pair, and this is deliberate: The line is half duplex and shared. Between an instruction and its status packet no other instruction may be sent, and a servo answers within a few hundred microseconds. A caller that starts a read and returns to do other work cannot send anything else on the bus until the reply is in, so the bus is blocked either way; splitting the call only moves the wait into the caller. The wait is short. A read of one servo at 1 Mbit/s takes well under a millisecond; at the default 57 600 bit/s about 5 ms. Config::reply_timeout_us bounds the wait for a servo that does not answer. Fast reads are the answer to many servos. SyncRead() and FastSyncRead() collect many servos in one transaction, so a control loop reads the whole arm in one call instead of one call per servo. A state machine would need a clock and an interrupt-safe line. Receiving into the driver from an ISR would put a lock or a lock-free queue into a library that has none. A port can still make Read() cooperative (an RTOS queue with a timeout, as the ESP32 port does), so other tasks run while the driver waits. Run the driver from one task, give it the bus, and use the Sync and Fast reads for the multi-servo case. If you need a call that never waits at all, wrap the driver in a task and talk to it with a queue; the driver stays blocking and the task decides what blocks. docs.text: Configuration ¶ Every field of dynamixel::Config , the presets, how a configuration is checked, and the optional Kconfig layer. Datasheet sections this page relies on From ROBOTIS e-Manual, DYNAMIXEL Protocol 2.0 web page, no revision mark: Byte to byte time and the packet gap: 1.6 Byte to Byte Time, p. 1 Response policy and the broadcast ID: 3.4 Response Policy, p. 1 All of them, with the driver API for each: Datasheet map . Fields ¶ Config{} suits a protocol 2.0 bus of X-series servos at their factory settings. The timing fields are driver side: the e-Manual gives no reply deadline, so these are the driver's own choices (see the Contract ). Fields with a unit carry it in the name. Field Default Range What it does protocol Protocol::V2 V1 , V2 Packet format of every servo on the bus baud 57 600 9 600 to 10 500 000 UART rate; applied through the port's SetBaudRate() when it has one reply_timeout_us 20 000 100 to 1 000 000 Longest wait for the first byte of a reply gap_timeout_us 5 000 100 to 1 000 000 Longest wait for the next bytes of a packet that has started reboot_wait_us 500 000 0 to 10 000 000 Wait after a Reboot, Restore or Factory Reset reply baud_change_wait_us 10 000 0 to 10 000 000 Wait after a servo's baud rate changed retries 1 0 to 5 Repeats of a ping or read after a missing, corrupted or invalid reply; writes are never repeated echo EchoMode::None None , Loopback Verify the echo of every sent byte on a single-wire bus alert_policy AlertPolicy::Report Report , Fail A hardware alert in a reply: succeed and latch it, or return DeviceFault status_return StatusReturn::All PingOnly , ReadOnly , All How much the servos answer; calls that need an answer the level does not give return Unsupported broadcast_timeout_us 100 000 100 to 1 000 000 Wait for each reply of a broadcast ping allow_destructive false Permit Factory Reset, Control Table Restore, Clear and ID writes to every servo Choose reply_timeout_us longer than the servos' Return Delay Time (500 microseconds at the factory value) plus the time the longest reply takes on the line. At 57 600 bit/s a byte takes 174 microseconds, so a 100-byte reply needs about 17 ms; the default 20 ms covers the reads of a few registers, and a Fast Sync Read of many servos at a low rate needs more. gap_timeout_us has to cover a pause inside a packet, such as the latency timer of a USB adapter. allow_destructive is never set from Kconfig: it is a decision made in code, where the consequence is visible. Presets ¶ Preset What it sets Use it for FastBusPreset() Reply wait 10 ms, gap 2 ms A short bus of servos that all answer, at a high rate UsbAdapterPreset() Reply wait 60 ms, gap 40 ms A bus behind a USB adapter with a 16 ms latency timer LegacyBusPreset() Protocol 1.0 at 1 Mbit/s AX, RX, DX and MX (1.0) servos at their factory rate Start from a preset or from Config{} and change fields: dynamixel :: Config LegacyConfig () { dynamixel :: Config c = dynamixel :: LegacyBusPreset (); // protocol 1.0 at 1 Mbit/s c . retries = 2 ; // repeat a lost ping or read twice c . reply_timeout_us = 5'000 ; // a short bus answers quickly return c ; // dynamixel::Validate(c) checks it without the bus } dynamixel :: Error StartLegacy ( MyPort & port ) { static dynamixel :: DYNAMIXEL < MyPort > servos ( port , LegacyConfig ()); // stored, no I/O return servos . EnsureInitialized (). error ; // InvalidArgument if the config is out of range } Validation ¶ dynamixel::Validate(config) checks a configuration without touching the bus, and EnsureInitialized() and ApplyConfig() call it before any I/O. It returns Error::InvalidArgument when an enum holds a value that is not an enumerator, the baud rate or a timeout is outside its range, a wait is above ten seconds, or retries is above 5. A configuration fixed at build time can be checked by the compiler instead: // A configuration fixed at build time: an invalid value stops the build instead of the first call. inline constexpr dynamixel :: CheckedConfig kBoard { dynamixel :: Config {. baud = 1'000'000 , . retries = 2 }}; CheckedConfig does not compile for an invalid value, so a wrong number stops the build and not the first call. docs.text: Contract ¶ What the DYNAMIXEL driver promises, what it needs, and the rules a caller follows. The driver inherits the Kokeb Labs driver contract ; this page states only what is specific to it. A change to anything here is a breaking change, listed under Breaking in the changelog . Promises ¶ The constructor is noexcept , stores the configuration, does no I/O and cannot fail. EnsureInitialized() is the only way to start the driver. Its first call checks the stored configuration ( InvalidArgument , nothing sent), brings the port up and applies Config::baud through SetBaudRate() when the port has it. It sends nothing on the bus. On any failure the driver stays uninitialised and the next call starts again from the beginning; once it has succeeded, later calls return Ok with no I/O. Before EnsureInitialized() succeeds, every call that would use the bus fails and sends nothing. The error is NotInitialized , except that an argument or permission problem is reported first: InvalidArgument , Unsupported (the protocol or family has no such call) and NotPermitted (a destructive call without Config::allow_destructive ) do not depend on the state of the bus, so they are returned whether or not the driver is up. In all of these cases nothing is sent. The torque-off calls DisableTorque() , DisableTorqueAll() , DisableTorqueEach() and DisableTorqueAt() , and Reboot() , are never refused for the driver's state: they start the port themselves when needed (and set the bus baud rate when the driver was not initialised), need no consent flag, and write even when the input flush fails (the fault is reported as Bus after the write). A torque-off is sent up to three times per servo: once when a trusted answer confirms it, three times when no answer can confirm it (status return level below 2, or the broadcast) or when the flush failed. They are the stop an emergency handler can call from any state. The only refusals are an argument the bus protocol does not have ( InvalidArgument : an ID out of range, a family that does not speak the bus protocol, an address above 255 in protocol 1.0, or a family with no torque register such as Generic : use DisableTorqueAt() with the servo's own Torque Enable address) and a port that cannot start. DisableTorqueEach() returns only the first error. On an invalid configuration they still run, with the timeouts held inside 100 microseconds to 1 second and the reboot wait inside 10 seconds. A typed call ( ReadRegister() , WriteRegister() , SetTorque() , ReadFeedback() , the stop) for a family that does not speak the bus protocol (for example an AX/RX/DX servo on a protocol 2.0 bus) is refused before anything is sent, because the same register name sits at another address in the other table. Every port failure propagates as Error::Bus ; no call returns a stale or zero value after a failed read, and a failed Result<T> always carries T{} . Every wait is bounded: a reply by Config::reply_timeout_us for the first byte and Config::gap_timeout_us per further read, a broadcast ping by Config::broadcast_timeout_us per reply, a reboot by Config::reboot_wait_us . Each receive is also bounded by a number of reads ( 4 * FrameBytes + 16 ), and a broadcast ping by one reply per ID, so no call can block forever, whatever the line carries (the fuzz targets check this with endless noise). The time bound is therefore steps times timeout, not one timeout: a line that gives one byte per read can hold a call for up to Config::reply_timeout_us + (4 * FrameBytes + 15) * Config::gap_timeout_us (about 2 000 s at the 1 s limit and the default 512-byte buffer), a stop for three times that, and a broadcast ping for that many times the reply count. Use short timeouts on a bus whose line you do not trust. A write is sent once. A ping or read is repeated up to Config::retries times after a missing, corrupted or invalid reply; nothing else is repeated, except the torque-off calls above. Config{} is a valid configuration for a protocol 2.0 bus at 57 600 bit/s. A missing, misdeclared or noexcept -less required hook is a compile error; a missing SetBaudRate() gives Unsupported from ChangeBusBaud() ; a missing Log() logs nothing. A multi-servo read ( SyncRead() , FastSyncRead() , BulkRead() , FastBulkRead() ) fills one DeviceReply per requested ID. When the call returns Ok , each device that is Ok has valid data in its slice of the output; the slices of the others are not meaningful. The driver never sends a destructive instruction (Factory Reset, Control Table Restore, Clear, an ID write to every servo) unless Config::allow_destructive is set. The driver sends a packet of at most FrameBytes bytes; GetLastRequest() returns the bytes as put on the line. Depends on ¶ Dependency Version Why A C++20 compiler GCC 10, Clang 13 or later Concepts constrain the port CMake 3.16 or later Generates dynamixel_version.h Your port A UART at 8N1 with the half-duplex direction handled ( Porting ), a delay, optionally the baud rate and logging Nothing else: no RTOS, no SDK, no other repository of the org. Threading ¶ The driver is not thread-safe and takes no lock. Use each driver object from one task at a time, or guard every call on it with one mutex; the layer that owns the driver owns that lock, and the bus lock when several driver objects share a UART. Nothing may run in an ISR: every call can block for a bus transfer or a delay. Separate objects share no state. Errors ¶ dynamixel::Error inside dynamixel::Result<T> . Values 0 to 9 are the shared base set; values from 16 are specific to the bus. Error Value Returned when Ok 0 The call succeeded NotInitialized 1 EnsureInitialized() has not succeeded, or Deinitialize() ran since InvalidArgument 2 A Config field or argument is out of range, or the packet does not fit FrameBytes ; nothing was sent Bus 3 A port hook returned false , or Read() returned more bytes than asked Timeout 4 No complete reply within the deadline (nothing, or a truncated packet) DeviceIdMismatch 5 The reply came from another ID than the one addressed, or the model differs Crc 6 The CRC-16 (protocol 2.0) or checksum (protocol 1.0) of the reply did not match Busy 7 Reserved by the shared set; this driver has no pending state and never returns it DeviceFault 8 The servo reported a hardware alert and AlertPolicy::Fail is set Unsupported 9 The protocol, family, register or port hook does not offer this call DeviceError 16 The servo rejected the instruction; GetLastReply() has the error number InvalidReply 17 A reply the protocol refuses: header, length, instruction or parameter count EchoMismatch 18 With EchoMode::Loopback , the sent bytes were not read back as sent LineFault 19 The line carried only 00 or only FF , or did not go quiet: stuck, floating NotPermitted 22 A destructive instruction without Config::allow_destructive The API guide says what to do about each. Memory ¶ No heap, no exceptions, no RTTI, no std::function , no std::string , no printf and no static mutable state. A driver object holds a reference to the port, a Config , two buffers of FrameBytes bytes (512 by default), a 64-byte scratch buffer, the last reply, the latched alert and the statistics: about 1.2 KB at the default size. The largest stack buffer of a call is 5 bytes; the multi-servo reads write into the caller's buffers. Platform ¶ Platform-free: the same code runs on any target with a C++20 compiler, including the host tests. The ESP-IDF port in examples/esp32 is an example, not part of the driver. Open points ¶ The e-Manual does not specify four behaviours that the driver has to decide. They are checked against the bus model, not against a servo; confirm them on hardware before relying on them: Point What the driver does The ID in the header of the first part of a Fast Sync Read or Fast Bulk Read Accepts any ID in the header and verifies the parts one by one The ID in the reply to a write of the ID register Accepts the old and the new ID How a silent servo shifts the replies of the servos after it in a Sync Read Matches every reply to its ID: a reply that belongs to a later servo marks the earlier ones Timeout , and the read goes on The reply deadline The driver's own: Config::reply_timeout_us , 20 ms by default Deviations from the standard ¶ None.

docs.text: Control tables ¶ Every servo has a control table: a block of registers that is read and written with the Read and Write instructions. The addresses and units differ by family. The driver keeps one table per family and one family-neutral name per register ( Reg ), so ReadRegister({id, family}, Reg::PresentPosition) works on any family that has one. A model number the catalogue does not list is Family::Generic : raw addresses only. The Pro, P, H, L and Y series are not in the catalogue: read them with raw addresses and Family::Generic . Kinds of value ¶ Each register has a Kind that says how its bytes decode: Kind Registers Decoding Unsigned most of them little-endian unsigned Signed position, velocity, current and offsets of protocol 2.0 families two's complement of the register width SignMag10 speed, load and torque of protocol 1.0 families bits 9 to 0 magnitude, bit 10 the direction Offset2048 current of the MX-64 and MX-106 (1.0) value minus 2048 WriteRegister() checks that the value fits the register and its kind ( InvalidArgument , nothing sent), refuses a read-only register, and returns Unsupported for a family without the register. Units ¶ Info(family) and FindModel(model) carry the unit of position, velocity and current: position: microdeg_per_count (for example 88 000 micro-degrees for the 4096-count families); velocity: mrpm_per_count (milli-rpm per count); current: ModelInfo::current_ua (micro-amperes per count, 0 when the table has no current register). ReadFeedback() returns position, velocity, effort (load in per mille, or current in counts: Feedback::EffortKind ), voltage in 0.1 V and temperature in degrees Celsius, read in one transfer. Indirect addresses ¶ The X430, X540, XW and MX(2.0) tables have indirect address and indirect data blocks: map up to 28 (or 56) scattered registers to one contiguous block, so that a single Read or Sync Read fetches them all. Baud rates ¶ SetServoBaudRate() writes the servo's Baud Rate register with the value its family's scheme encodes ( BaudValueFor() ), and ChangeBusBaud() then moves the UART. The divider families encode 2 000 000 / (value + 1) ; the table families list 9 600, 57 600, 115 200, 1 000 000, 2 000 000, 3 000 000, 4 000 000 and 4 500 000 bit/s as the e-Manual does for their model.

docs.text: Each register has a Kind that says how its bytes decode: Kind Registers Decoding Unsigned most of them little-endian unsigned Signed position, velocity, current and offsets of protocol 2.0 families two's complement of the register width SignMag10 speed, load and torque of protocol 1.0 families bits 9 to 0 magnitude, bit 10 the direction Offset2048 current of the MX-64 and MX-106 (1.0) value minus 2048 WriteRegister() checks that the value fits the register and its kind ( InvalidArgument , nothing sent), refuses a read-only register, and returns Unsupported for a family without the register.
docs.title: Kinds of value

docs.text: Info(family) and FindModel(model) carry the unit of position, velocity and current: position: microdeg_per_count (for example 88 000 micro-degrees for the 4096-count families); velocity: mrpm_per_count (milli-rpm per count); current: ModelInfo::current_ua (micro-amperes per count, 0 when the table has no current register). ReadFeedback() returns position, velocity, effort (load in per mille, or current in counts: Feedback::EffortKind ), voltage in 0.1 V and temperature in degrees Celsius, read in one transfer.
docs.title: Units

docs.text: The X430, X540, XW and MX(2.0) tables have indirect address and indirect data blocks: map up to 28 (or 56) scattered registers to one contiguous block, so that a single Read or Sync Read fetches them all. Indirect(family, index) gives the addresses of the pair index (1 to 28 in the first block, to 56 in the second block above address 255); Info(family).indirect_blocks says how many blocks a family has.

docs.text: SetServoBaudRate() writes the servo's Baud Rate register with the value its family's scheme encodes ( BaudValueFor() ), and ChangeBusBaud() then moves the UART. The divider families encode 2 000 000 / (value + 1) ; the table families list 9 600, 57 600, 115 200, 1 000 000, 2 000 000, 3 000 000, 4 000 000 and 4 500 000 bit/s as the e-Manual does for their model.

docs.text: Hardware ¶ How a DYNAMIXEL servo bus is wired and timed, as the driver uses it: the connector, the half-duplex data line, the bus settings, the timing and the supply. The driver talks to a family of servos, not to one chip. The reference part of this page is the XM430-W350; the other families differ in the connector housing and the supply range ( Control tables ). Not verified on hardware: everything here follows the ROBOTIS e-Manual, which is a set of web pages (see the Datasheet map ). Datasheet sections this page relies on Half duplex line and Tx/Rx direction: ROBOTIS e-Manual, DYNAMIXEL Protocol 2.0 web page, no revision mark, 1.4 Half Duplex; 1.5 Tx, Rx Direction, p. 1 Specifications, baud rates and ID range: ROBOTIS e-Manual, XM430-W350 web page, no revision mark, 1 Specifications, p. 1 Connector, power and communication circuit: ROBOTIS e-Manual, XM430-W350 web page, no revision mark, 4.5 Connector Information; 4.6 Communication Circuit, p. 1 Connector and half-duplex circuit, protocol 1.0 servos: ROBOTIS e-Manual, AX-12A web page, no revision mark, 5.2 Connector Information; 5.4 Communication Circuit, p. 1 All of them, with the driver API for each: Datasheet map . The servos need their own supply The XM430-W350 runs from 10.0 V to 14.8 V (12.0 V recommended) and draws amperes when it moves. Never power it from the MCU board. The TTL connector carries a single TTL data line (the e-Manual's text gives no voltage level; its circuit figure pulls the line up to 5 V, see Circuits below); the RS-485 variant is differential and needs a transceiver. Pins ¶ The 3-pin TTL connector of the X series (JST EH) carries ground, the supply and one half-duplex data line. The RS-485 variant has the same first two pins and splits the data into DATA+ and DATA-. DYNAMIXEL pinout, TTL servo Figure description and sources The DYNAMIXEL seen from the top, in its TTL servo package. Pin 1 is marked by the dot; the numbers run counter-clockwise from it. Each pad is coloured by the pin's electrical type (legend below). Next to it is the pin's name and, in mono, the hook of the driver's port that drives or reads it; a pin without a hook is not used by the driver. Drawn from: docs/hardware.yml ; inc/dynamixel_uart_interface.hpp . TTL servo, 3 pins (4.5 Connector Information, p. 1). Pin Name Type (domain) Function Driver hook Datasheet 1 GND ground Ground and the negative supply (pin 1 of the connector) - 4.5, p. 1 2 VDD power (VDD) Positive supply, 10.0 V to 14.8 V, 12.0 V recommended (XM430-W350) - 1, p. 1 3 DATA open drain (TTL, 5 V in the circuit) Half-duplex TTL data line, 8N1: the master and every servo share it. The master's TX and RX meet here (single wire), so a sent byte is also read back unless the adapter gates it. The page text gives no voltage level; the circuit figure shows a 10 kOhm pull-up to 5 V. Unverified: the drive type (open drain) is not stated Write() 4.5, p. 1 Source of this table and of the chip figures: docs/hardware.yml . The driver has no pin of its own to drive: the only hooks are Write() and Read() of your UART port. The direction of the half-duplex stage is part of Write() ( Porting ). The data line ¶ All servos and the master share one data line. The master sends an instruction packet; the addressed servo answers with a status packet after its Return Delay Time (500 microseconds at the factory value, up to 508). Between the two the line must be turned round: the master stops driving it and listens. Wiring How the direction is switched Port Config::echo UART with a direction pin (RS-485 transceiver, tri-state buffer) The UART's RTS output or a GPIO, high while sending Write() raises it, sends, waits for the last stop bit and lowers it None UART with a hardware half-duplex mode (ESP32 UART_MODE_RS485_HALF_DUPLEX ) The hardware, with the first start bit and after the last stop bit Write() sends and waits for the transmitter to be done None TX and RX tied to the single wire (open-drain or diode stage) None: the master's own bytes come back on RX Write() leaves the echo in the receive FIFO Loopback With EchoMode::Loopback the driver reads the echo of every packet it sent and compares it with the request: another talker on the line, or a short, shows as Error::EchoMismatch before any reply is waited for. sequenceDiagram participant Master as MCU (driver) participant Servo as Servo 1 Master->>Servo: Read 4 bytes at address 132 (instruction packet) Note over Master,Servo: Return Delay Time, factory 500 microseconds Servo-->>Master: Status packet with the 4 bytes (error byte, CRC-16) Bus settings ¶ Setting Value UART format 8 data bits, no parity, 1 stop bit Bit rate About 7 800 (AX-12A) or 9 600 to 4 500 000 bit/s on the catalogued families; factory 57 600 (X series) or 1 000 000 (protocols 1.0 families); every servo on the bus must run the same rate Packet Protocol 1.0 or 2.0, the same for every servo on the bus ( Protocol ) Byte gap inside an instruction At most 1.5 ms in protocol 2.0 and 100 ms in protocol 1.0, or the servo drops the packet: Write() sends the packet in one go IDs 0 to 252 (2.0) or 0 to 253 (1.0); 254 is the broadcast ID; every ID on a bus must be unique The factory bit rate and ID differ by family: an X-series servo comes at ID 1 and 57 600 bit/s, an AX-12A at ID 1 and 1 000 000 bit/s. Config::baud must match; a wrong rate looks like silence ( Error::Timeout ) or noise. Circuits ¶ DYNAMIXEL: servo bus on an MCU's UART through a half-duplex stage Figure description and sources A schematic. The MCU is on the left, each of its pins level with the chip pin it connects to; above each wire is the hook of the driver's port that drives or reads it. Supply pins point up to their supply and decoupling, ground pins down. Pins on the right carry the loads and the pins tied to a supply or ground; a cross marks a pin left open. A dot is a junction; wires that cross without a dot are not connected. Drawn from: docs/hardware.yml ; inc/dynamixel_uart_interface.hpp . The e-Manual's recommended TTL circuit is a pair of tri-state buffers (a 74LVC2G241 in the figure), one for each direction. One direction signal ( TX_Enable ) drives both enables: low enables the receive buffer (servo DATA to the MCU's RXD), high enables the transmit buffer (the MCU's TXD to DATA). The circuit is a figure only: the page text says that it "is designed for 5V or 5V tolerant MCU. Otherwise, use a Level Shifter to match the voltage of MCU", and the figure runs the buffers from 5 V. It has a 10 kilohm pull-up to 5 V on the RXD node and on the DATA node, and a 10 kilohm pull- down to ground on TX_Enable , so that the stage listens while the MCU pin is not driven. Do not copy the enable resistor as a pull-up: a pull-up on the direction pin would enable the transmit buffer and drive DATA high at idle, against the servos' own answers. A 3.3 V MCU therefore needs a level shifter ; the e-Manual shows no 3.3 V circuit. What is read from the figure (the part name, the 5 V supply, the pull-ups and the pull-down) is unverified against a second source. The stage drawn here is a block, not a part; any circuit that gives the same behaviour (an RS-485 transceiver with the right level, or a UART's own half-duplex mode) works the same way for the driver. Add a bulk capacitor on the servo supply; the 100 microfarad of the drawing is an example, not a datasheet value. docs.text: All servos and the master share one data line. The master sends an instruction packet; the addressed servo answers with a status packet after its Return Delay Time (500 microseconds at the factory value, up to 508). Between the two the line must be turned round: the master stops driving it and listens. docs.text: DYNAMIXEL: servo bus on an MCU's UART through a half-duplex stage Figure description and sources A schematic. The MCU is on the left, each of its pins level with the chip pin it connects to; above each wire is the hook of the driver's port that drives or reads it. Supply pins point up to their supply and decoupling, ground pins down. Pins on the right carry the loads and the pins tied to a supply or ground; a cross marks a pin left open. A dot is a junction; wires that cross without a dot are not connected. Drawn from: docs/hardware.yml ; inc/dynamixel_uart_interface.hpp . The e-Manual's recommended TTL circuit is a pair of tri-state buffers (a 74LVC2G241 in the figure), one for each direction. One direction signal ( TX_Enable ) drives both enables: low enables the receive buffer (servo DATA to the MCU's RXD), high enables the transmit buffer (the MCU's TXD to DATA). The circuit is a figure only: the page text says that it "is designed for 5V or 5V tolerant MCU. Otherwise, use a Level Shifter to match the voltage of MCU", and the figure runs the buffers from 5 V. It has a 10 kilohm pull-up to 5 V on the RXD node and on the DATA node, and a 10 kilohm pull- down to ground on TX_Enable , so that the stage listens while the MCU pin is not driven. Do not copy the enable resistor as a pull-up: a pull-up on the direction pin would enable the transmit buffer and drive DATA high at idle, against the servos' own answers. A 3.3 V MCU therefore needs a level shifter ; the e-Manual shows no 3.3 V circuit. What is read from the figure (the part name, the 5 V supply, the pull-ups and the pull-down) is unverified against a second source. The stage drawn here is a block, not a part; any circuit that gives the same behaviour (an RS-485 transceiver with the right level, or a UART's own half-duplex mode) works the same way for the driver. Add a bulk capacitor on the servo supply; the 100 microfarad of the drawing is an example, not a datasheet value.

docs.text: Installation ¶ Add the driver to a CMake project on any MCU or on your PC, or to an ESP-IDF project. It is a header-only C++20 library with no dependencies, and one root CMakeLists.txt serves every build. Requirements ¶ A C++20 compiler: GCC 10+, Clang 13+ or a current MSVC. The driver uses concepts and requires . CMake 3.16 or later: it generates the version header the driver includes ( dynamixel_version.h ). No RTOS, heap, exceptions or RTTI: every call is noexcept and returns a Result . Get the source ¶ A git submodule keeps the driver pinned to the version you chose: git submodule add https://github.com/kokeb-labs-drivers/driver-dynamixel.git external/driver-dynamixel git submodule update --init external/driver-dynamixel Only inc/ , src/ , cmake/ , _config/ and CMakeLists.txt are needed to build. The examples are not; the ESP32 example even has its own submodule ( examples/esp32/scripts ). CMake (any MCU, any host) ¶ This is the MCU-neutral path: the same two lines work for a host build, STM32 (CubeMX CMake projects), RP2040 (Pico SDK), nRF (nRF Connect SDK) or any other CMake toolchain. Platforms lists what has a port today. add_subdirectory ( external/driver-dynamixel ) target_link_libraries ( my_app PRIVATE dynamixel::dynamixel ) dynamixel::dynamixel is an alias of the dynamixel INTERFACE target. It carries the include directories (the headers and the generated version header) and requires C++20, so your target does not need to set either. Option Default Effect DYNAMIXEL_ENABLE_WARNINGS OFF -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic on every target that links the driver DYNAMIXEL_BUILD_TESTS OFF Builds the host tests in tests/ and the host example ( Testing and CI ) Installed package ¶ To use the driver without adding its source tree to your build, install it and find the package: cmake -S external/driver-dynamixel -B build-dynamixel cmake --install build-dynamixel --prefix /opt/sdk find_package ( dynamixel 0.1 REQUIRED ) # with CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH=/opt/sdk target_link_libraries ( my_app PRIVATE dynamixel::dynamixel ) The target is dynamixel::dynamixel in both cases ( EXPORT_NAME ), so a project can switch between add_subdirectory() and find_package() without changing its target_link_libraries() . The headers and the generated dynamixel_version.h go to include/dynamixel/inc/ , the template implementation to include/dynamixel/src/dynamixel.ipp . The host CI installs the package and builds a consumer against it on every pull request ( Testing and CI ). ESP-IDF ¶ Under ESP-IDF the root CMakeLists.txt registers the repository itself as a component: with ESP_PLATFORM set it calls idf_component_register() from the same build settings, with the menu in _config/Kconfig . There is no wrapper to copy. ESP-IDF names a component after its folder, so the name in your REQUIRES is the name of the folder the repository is in. Pick one of these: How What to write Component name Folder of extra components list(APPEND EXTRA_COMPONENT_DIRS external/driver-dynamixel) in the project CMakeLists.txt , before project.cmake driver-dynamixel (the folder) Submodule under components/ git submodule add https://github.com/kokeb-labs-drivers/driver-dynamixel.git components/dynamixel dynamixel (the folder) Component manager, from git The dependency below in main/idf_component.yml dynamixel (the key) # main/idf_component.yml of your project dependencies : dynamixel : git : https://github.com/kokeb-labs-drivers/driver-dynamixel.git version : v0.1.0 # a release tag Your component then declares REQUIRES dynamixel (or the folder name), and idf.py menuconfig shows the driver's menu ( Configuration ). The ESP32 example uses the first way, with EXTRA_COMPONENT_DIRS pointing at the repository root, and works out the folder name in main/CMakeLists.txt ; CI builds it on every pull request. The repository has no idf_component.yml . The component manager does not need one for a git dependency; the manifest is only required to publish to the ESP Component Registry, which these releases do not use. If registry publishing is chosen, the manifest is added at the root then. How the build is organised ¶ Layer File Role Settings cmake/dynamixel_build_settings.cmake Target name, include directories, sources, version: the single source of truth Library CMakeLists.txt INTERFACE target, alias, install rules and the package export, or the ESP-IDF component Tool configuration _config/ Doxyfile, the docs site, Kconfig, clang-format, clang-tidy and the linters Version ¶ The version is set once in the settings file and written into dynamixel_version.h in the build tree at configure time. The Doxyfile ( _config/Doxyfile ) carries a copy; a host test fails when it differs. Read it at run time: const char * v = dynamixel :: GetDriverVersion (); // "0.1.0" Next ¶ Quickstart runs the driver on your PC, then on your MCU; Porting writes the port for your MCU.

docs.text: Mechanization policy ¶ Where each defect class of the catalogue is caught, and how a class moves to a cheaper catch. The goal: a defect is found by the cheapest check that can find it, and reviewers spend their time on judgement, not on what a script can do. Decision rule ¶ Catch a class at the first level that can decide it without judgement, in order of cost: Lint ( tools/preflight.sh , runs in seconds, on every builder's machine). Use it when the defect is a pattern in text or syntax: a forbidden include, a MISRA rule CodeQL reports, a missing else , a parameter name, a symbol named in docs that does not exist, a missing gitlink. Test, model or mutation (host tests, the chip model's fault knobs, fuzz properties, compile-fail cases, mutants of a fix). Use it when the defect is behaviour: what the driver sends or returns when the chip or the bus misbehaves. A test is the right level when the model can be made to misbehave in exactly that way. Independent review question (a reviewer who did not write the code). Use it only for what needs judgement: whether the datasheet was read correctly, whether a state machine is complete, whether the model is independent of the driver, whether a doc claim is true. Every catalogue entry names its level under DETECTION. A class with no lint or test is a review class and costs reviewer time every round; it is a candidate for promotion. Promotion ¶ A defect that reached a reviewer or the CI of a second driver is promoted one level up: review to test, test to lint where a pattern exists. The reviewer who finds the second occurrence writes the promotion item in the round's report; the template maintainer (the agent or person that owns the template branch) implements it before the next driver's first push, or records why it cannot be mechanised in the catalogue entry. A defect that reached a third driver after its promotion means the check is wrong: fix the check first, then look at the driver. Demotion never happens by silence: a check is removed only with a catalogue note saying what replaced it. What a lint may and may not do ¶ It reports file:line , the catalogue id, and the fix. It exits non-zero on a finding, in the preflight and the gate. It has no false-positive tolerance : before merging, it runs over every finished driver and the template; any finding on a driver that CI shows clean is a false positive, and the lint is not merged until it has none (narrow the pattern; do not add an ignore list per driver). It may be conservative the other way (miss cases): then the catalogue says partial and names the review question that covers the rest. It never edits files, never skips silently (a missing tool is reported as a skipped step in the final line, and the gate treats a skipped MISRA or ESP32 step as a failure), and has a selftest with one bad and one good case. It does not replace the CI scan: CI is the final word for MISRA. Recording a new finding ¶ Append the finding to its catalogue entry (driver, review round or CI report file, finding id) and update the count and the index table; add a new entry only when no class fits. Write the check at the level the rules above give: the lint, or the test pattern (model knob, mutant, fuzz property), or the reviewer's question in the skill. Run it over the finished drivers (lint) or add the regression test that fails without the fix (test). Add a CHANGELOG.md entry under [Unreleased] and the template change is released as a new template commit; drivers take it with scaffold.py --check-drift --fix (the skills and tools are managed files), which updates the template pin in .kokeb/template.yml . Mention the catalogue id in the commit subject. The pre-push gate ¶ A driver is cleared for its first push only by kokeb-tools/gate.sh <chip> (the orchestrator's script, one run per driver through the shared Docker lock). It writes a log and a verdict, and PASS needs all of: container preflight ( tools/preflight.sh --container ) with 0 failure(s) and 0 gate failure(s) , including the MISRA scan and the ESP32 builds; a skipped MISRA or ESP32 step is a FAIL; handbook_check reports 0 errors (this includes the library-subset include scan); tools/check_standalone.py passes; template drift: scaffold.py --check-drift reports nothing; no .pdf file is tracked; the examples/esp32/scripts gitlink (mode 160000) is present; the tree is staged as it will be committed. No silent skips: every step prints a line, and a missing tool fails the gate. Roles ¶ Builders write code, models, tests and docs and run host tests and the quick preflight. They do not run the container gate, push, or create repositories. The gate runner is one serialized worker that runs gate.sh for one driver at a time and reports the verdict and the log; it does not edit the driver. Reviewers are read-only and independent. They are given the code, the model, the datasheet, the catalogue and the previous round's report, and never the builder's conclusions (the build report is read only in the claims-vs-code step). They run the review-round protocol. Fixers change the driver, fix at the cause, add the test that fails without the fix, and answer each finding id. The template maintainer applies promotions and keeps the catalogue current. Backlog of promotions (state of the catalogue) ¶ The classes whose target level is above their present level are listed in the catalogue index: RD-12 to RD-18 and RD-23 (MISRA patterns, one misra_lint with a rule per id), RD-20 and RD-22 (ESP-IDF and compile-fail lints), RD-08 ( claims-symbols ), RD-07 (model standalone lint), RD-06, RD-01, RD-02, RD-03, RD-05, RD-10 and RD-25 (shared model knobs and a template mutation runner), RD-21 (host start-up test of the ESP32 port).

docs.text: Porting ¶ Write the platform port: one class that brings the UART up and moves bytes, plus the half-duplex direction. This page lists the hooks, the rules a port follows and how to check it. Datasheet sections this page relies on Half duplex line and Tx/Rx direction: ROBOTIS e-Manual, DYNAMIXEL Protocol 2.0 web page, no revision mark, 1.4 Half Duplex; 1.5 Tx, Rx Direction, p. 1 Byte to byte time and the packet gap: ROBOTIS e-Manual, DYNAMIXEL Protocol 2.0 web page, no revision mark, 1.6 Byte to Byte Time, p. 1 Connector and half-duplex circuit, protocol 1.0 servos: ROBOTIS e-Manual, AX-12A web page, no revision mark, 5.2 Connector Information; 5.4 Communication Circuit, p. 1 All of them, with the driver API for each: Datasheet map . The driver never calls your SDK. It calls hooks on a class you derive from dynamixel::UartInterface<Self> (in inc/dynamixel_uart_interface.hpp ). The base uses CRTP and declares no hook itself; the driver template is constrained by the dynamixel::UartPort concept, so calls are resolved at compile time (no virtual functions, nothing to allocate) and a missing or misdeclared hook is a compile error at the point of use. What you implement ¶ Method Required Contract bool EnsureInitialized() noexcept yes Bring the UART up at 8 data bits, no parity, 1 stop bit; return true at once afterwards. false makes the driver's EnsureInitialized() return Bus bool Write(const uint8_t* data, std::size_t len) noexcept yes Switch the line to transmit, send all len bytes without gaps, wait until the last stop bit has left the shift register, switch back to receive; false on an error std::size_t Read(uint8_t* data, std::size_t max, uint32_t timeout_us) noexcept yes Return 1 to max bytes as soon as one is there, waiting at most timeout_us for the first; 0 when none arrived bool FlushInput() noexcept yes Drop every received byte not returned by Read() yet void DelayUs(uint32_t us) noexcept yes Wait at least us microseconds (reboot and baud change settle times) bool SetBaudRate(uint32_t baud) noexcept no Reconfigure the UART; without it the port keeps its own rate void Log(LogLevel, const char* message) noexcept no Print one line; message is plain text, never a format string The port ¶ my_port.hpp class MyPort : public dynamixel :: UartInterface < MyPort > { public : // Bring the UART up once; later calls return true at once. bool EnsureInitialized () noexcept { if ( ! ready_ ) { ready_ = platform_uart_init (); } return ready_ ; } // Transmit the whole packet in one go, wait for the last stop bit, then listen again. bool Write ( const uint8_t * data , std :: size_t len ) noexcept { return platform_uart_send ( data , len ); } // One to `max` bytes as soon as one has arrived, or 0 after `timeout_us` without a byte. std :: size_t Read ( uint8_t * data , std :: size_t max , uint32_t timeout_us ) noexcept { return platform_uart_receive ( data , max , timeout_us ); } // Drop whatever has been received and not yet read. bool FlushInput () noexcept { return platform_uart_discard_input (); } // Wait at least `us` microseconds (the settle times after a reboot or a baud rate change). void DelayUs ( uint32_t us ) noexcept { platform_delay_us ( us ); } private : bool ready_ = false ; }; Rules the port must follow: Raw bytes only. The driver builds the packets, checks their CRC and finds the reply; the port does not parse or retry. Read() returns what is there. It does not wait for max bytes: one byte is enough to return, and the driver calls it again for the rest of the packet. A Read() that returns more than max is a Bus error. Read() rounds the timeout up. On an RTOS the tick may be a millisecond: round timeout_us up to a tick, at least one, and never wait less than asked. Write() sends the packet in one go. A pause longer than 1.5 ms between two bytes of a protocol 2.0 instruction (100 ms in protocol 1.0) makes the servo drop the packet. Do not send byte by byte from a slow loop. Write() waits for the last stop bit before it switches the line to receive. Returning when the transmit buffer is empty is too early: the last byte is still in the shift register, and cutting it off corrupts the CRC. Do not let an interrupt delay the turnaround. The servo answers after its Return Delay Time (500 microseconds at the factory value); a port that switches back to receive late loses the start of the reply. FlushInput() really flushes : the driver calls it before each request so a stale byte cannot shift a reply. Single wire, TX and RX tied: leave the echo of the sent bytes in the receive FIFO and set Config::echo = EchoMode::Loopback ; the driver reads it back and compares it. 8N1 , no flow control, at the rate of Config::baud . Bus requirements ¶ The driver states what the servos need from the line as constexpr values in inc/dynamixel_uart_interface.hpp (handbook KB-CPP-123). Check your port's settings against them with static_assert , as the ESP32 port does: Constant Value Meaning (e-Manual, protocols 1.0 and 2.0) kMaxBaudRate 4 500 000 The fastest rate of the catalogued families (the P series goes to 10.5 Mbit/s) kFactoryBaudRate 57 600 Factory rate of the X series kTurnaroundUs 500 Return Delay Time at its factory value (250 counts of 2 microseconds) kMaxTurnaroundUs 508 Largest Return Delay Time (254 counts) kInstructionByteGapMaxUsV2 1 500 Longest pause inside a protocol 2.0 instruction packet kInstructionByteGapMaxUsV1 100 000 Longest pause inside a protocol 1.0 instruction packet Direction control ¶ All servos share one data line, so the master must stop driving it while a servo answers. Pick one: Hardware Port UART with a hardware half-duplex mode (ESP32, many STM32 parts) Enable it; Write() is the plain send plus the wait for the transmitter A direction GPIO or RTS on an RS-485 transceiver or a tri-state buffer Write() raises it, sends, waits for the shift register and lowers it TX and RX tied to one wire with an open-drain stage Nothing to switch; the echo comes back, so set Config::echo = EchoMode::Loopback See Hardware for the circuits. Optional hooks ¶ The driver finds the optional hooks at compile time with C++20 requires , in one place ( dynamixel::detail ), and checks the exact signature. A missing hook falls back in a documented, safe way; a hook declared with the wrong type does not compile. Hook Used for Without it SetBaudRate() EnsureInitialized() , ApplyConfig() and ChangeBusBaud() set the UART rate The port's own rate stays; ChangeBusBaud() returns Unsupported Log() One line per lifecycle event or failure Nothing is logged A port with both hooks: class FullPort : public dynamixel :: UartInterface < FullPort > { public : bool EnsureInitialized () noexcept { return platform_uart_init (); } // Half duplex through a direction pin: transmit, wait for the last stop bit, listen again. bool Write ( const uint8_t * data , std :: size_t len ) noexcept { if ( ! platform_direction_transmit ( true )) { return false ; } const bool sent = platform_uart_send ( data , len ); // returns when the shift register is empty const bool listening = platform_direction_transmit ( false ); return sent && listening ; } std :: size_t Read ( uint8_t * data , std :: size_t max , uint32_t timeout_us ) noexcept { return platform_uart_receive ( data , max , timeout_us ); } bool FlushInput () noexcept { return platform_uart_discard_input (); } void DelayUs ( uint32_t us ) noexcept { platform_delay_us ( us ); } // Optional: lets ApplyConfig() and ChangeBusBaud() move the UART to a new rate. bool SetBaudRate ( uint32_t baud ) noexcept { return platform_uart_set_baud ( baud ); } // Optional: one line per lifecycle event or failure. The driver never formats; the port does. void Log ( dynamixel :: LogLevel level , const char * message ) noexcept { if ( level == dynamixel :: LogLevel :: Error ) { platform_log ( message ); // plain text: never use it as a format string } else { return ; } } }; A SetBaudRate() that returns void , or lacks noexcept , is a compile error: the driver must see a failed reconfiguration. The compile-fail tests check this. Reference implementations ¶ Every port lives with its example, in examples/<platform>/ ; the driver has none. Platforms lists them and how to add one. examples/host/host_dynamixel_port.hpp : any PC, against a simulated bus. Start from it for a host build or a test bench; it is also the smallest complete port. examples/esp32/main/esp32_dynamixel_port.hpp : ESP-IDF, the UART in RS-485 half-duplex mode with both hooks. Start from it for any ESP-IDF target. Not verified on hardware. Check your port ¶ Build it: the ports on this page are compiled by the host CI from tests/docs/ , with the driver instantiated over them. Call EnsureInitialized() : Ok proves the UART came up. Call Ping() on a servo whose ID you know: Ok proves that writes and reads work and the direction control turns the line round. Timeout is the servo's ID, rate, protocol or power; LineFault or EchoMismatch is the wiring ( Troubleshooting ). Threads ¶ The driver is not thread-safe. Give each driver object one owner task, or guard every call with one mutex. When several driver objects share a UART, the port must also serialise the bus. See Contract . Editor setup ¶ The clang-format and clang-tidy configuration is in _config/ , and the repository root has no copy of it. Tools that take a path use it directly; CI does the same: Tool Setting Command line clang-format --style=file:_config/.clang-format , clang-tidy --config-file=_config/.clang-tidy -p build VS Code (C/C++ extension) "C_Cpp.clang_format_style": "file:${workspaceFolder}/_config/.clang-format" and "C_Cpp.codeAnalysis.clangTidy.args": ["--config-file=${workspaceFolder}/_config/.clang-tidy"] clangd (VS Code clangd, Neovim, Emacs), CLion These find .clang-format and .clang-tidy only by name, from the file upwards: copy both to the root once ( cp _config/.clang-format _config/.clang-tidy . ). .gitignore lists the copies, so they never reach a commit; copy again after _config/ changes Configure with -DCMAKE_EXPORT_COMPILE_COMMANDS=ON (clangd: --compile-commands-dir=build ) so the editor sees the same flags as the build.

It does not wait for max bytes: one byte is enough to return, and the driver calls it again for the rest of the packet. A Read() that returns more than max is a Bus error. Read() rounds the timeout up. On an RTOS the tick may be a millisecond: round timeout_us up to a tick, at least one, and never wait less than asked. Write() sends the packet in one go. A pause longer than 1.5 ms between two bytes of a protocol 2.0 instruction (100 ms in protocol 1.0) makes the servo drop the packet. Do not send byte by byte from a slow loop. Write() waits for the last stop bit before it switches the line to receive. Returning when the transmit buffer is empty is too early: the last byte is still in the shift register, and cutting it off corrupts the CRC. Do not let an interrupt delay the turnaround. The servo answers after its Return Delay Time (500 microseconds at the factory value); a port that switches back to receive late loses the start of the reply. FlushInput() really flushes : the driver calls it before each request so a stale byte cannot shift a reply. Single wire, TX and RX tied: leave the echo of the sent bytes in the receive FIFO and set Config::echo = EchoMode::Loopback ; the driver reads it back and compares it. 8N1 , no flow control, at the rate of Config::baud .

docs.text: All servos share one data line, so the master must stop driving it while a servo answers. Pick one: Hardware Port UART with a hardware half-duplex mode (ESP32, many STM32 parts) Enable it; Write() is the plain send plus the wait for the transmitter A direction GPIO or RTS on an RS-485 transceiver or a tri-state buffer Write() raises it, sends, waits for the shift register and lowers it TX and RX tied to one wire with an open-drain stage Nothing to switch; the echo comes back, so set Config::echo = EchoMode::Loopback See Hardware for the circuits.

docs.text: The driver finds the optional hooks at compile time with C++20 requires , in one place ( dynamixel::detail ), and checks the exact signature. A missing hook falls back in a documented, safe way; a hook declared with the wrong type does not compile. Hook Used for Without it SetBaudRate() EnsureInitialized() , ApplyConfig() and ChangeBusBaud() set the UART rate The port's own rate stays; ChangeBusBaud() returns Unsupported Log() One line per lifecycle event or failure Nothing is logged A port with both hooks: class FullPort : public dynamixel :: UartInterface < FullPort > { public : bool EnsureInitialized () noexcept { return platform_uart_init (); } // Half duplex through a direction pin: transmit, wait for the last stop bit, listen again. bool Write ( const uint8_t * data , std :: size_t len ) noexcept { if ( ! platform_direction_transmit ( true )) { return false ; } const bool sent = platform_uart_send ( data , len ); // returns when the shift register is empty const bool listening = platform_direction_transmit ( false ); return sent && listening ; } std :: size_t Read ( uint8_t * data , std :: size_t max , uint32_t timeout_us ) noexcept { return platform_uart_receive ( data , max , timeout_us ); } bool FlushInput () noexcept { return platform_uart_discard_input (); } void DelayUs ( uint32_t us ) noexcept { platform_delay_us ( us ); } // Optional: lets ApplyConfig() and ChangeBusBaud() move the UART to a new rate. bool SetBaudRate ( uint32_t baud ) noexcept { return platform_uart_set_baud ( baud ); } // Optional: one line per lifecycle event or failure. The driver never formats; the port does. void Log ( dynamixel :: LogLevel level , const char * message ) noexcept { if ( level == dynamixel :: LogLevel :: Error ) { platform_log ( message ); // plain text: never use it as a format string } else { return ; } } }; A SetBaudRate() that returns void , or lacks noexcept , is a compile error: the driver must see a failed reconfiguration. The compile-fail tests check this.
